name: Shetani (Spirit Carvings)
description: Shetani (singular and plural in English, mashetani in Swahili) are spirits of East African mythology prevalent in Mozambique, particularly among the Makonde people of the northern Cabo Delgado province. These are mostly malevolent entities that manifest in a bewildering variety of forms with different powers and attributes. Physically, shetani of various types appear as distorted human and animal figures, often with exaggerated features, multiple limbs, or hybrid forms combining human and animal characteristics. What makes Mozambique's shetani tradition particularly distinctive is the extraordinary wood carving tradition that depicts them. Makonde carvers are world-renowned for their intricate representations of shetani in ebony and other hardwoods, creating art that is both aesthetically powerful and spiritually significant. The shetani are believed to inhabit remote forests, baobab trees, caves, and abandoned places. Encounters with shetani are reported cyclically, with specific 'panic' periods generating widespread fear. The word shetani derives from the Arabic shaitan (devil), reflecting the fusion of Islamic and indigenous Bantu spirit beliefs
source: Wikipedia; mythlok.com

name: Shuten-dōji
description: Leader of oni in Mt. The most powerful oni in Japan, feared as one of Japan's 'Three Great Evil Yokai' (日本三大悪妖怪) alongside Tamamo-no-Mae and Emperor Sutoku. His name 'Shuten' means 'sake drinker' - he's called the 'King of Drinking' for his legendary love of alcohol. He commanded hundreds of oni from his mountain stronghold, kidnapping young women from Kyoto to serve as his concubines or be devoured at his gruesome banquets. In the 14th-century Ōeyama Ekotoba scroll, he was identified by diviner Abe no Seimei as the culprit behind the disappearances. The Emperor commissioned Minamoto no Yorimitsu (Raikō) to defeat him—disguised as yamabushi (mountain priests), they offered demon-poison sake (jinben kidokusake) given by gods, and beheaded Shuten-dōji during a night raid. Remarkably, his severed head still lived and tried to bite Yorimitsu—only prevented by the hero wearing multiple helmets
source: Japanese folklore — Shuten-dōji is the demon king of Japanese oral tradition.

name: Si'lah
description: The Si'lah (also Sila or Si'lat, plural Sa'aali) is a female shapeshifting jinn from pre-Islamic Arabian folklore, particularly associated with the Bedouin tribes of the Arabian Peninsula including modern-day Saudi Arabia. Unlike the more generic Ghul, the Si'lah is specifically female and known primarily for seduction and shapeshifting. Si'lahs are described as the most intelligent and talented shapeshifters among the jinn, able to perfectly mimic human appearance — unlike the Ghul with its telltale donkey hooves. They prefer living near water sources in remote desert areas and oases. Si'lahs are notably amorous, often seeking human mates and bearing hybrid offspring called 'Bonoo.' In pre-Islamic legend, there was said to be a tribe called Banu Si'lat descended from a human-Si'lah union. The Si'lah represents the archetype of the dangerous seductive female spirit found across world cultures. Al-Qazwini noted that wolves are natural predators of the Si'lah
source: Al-Qazwini, Wonders of Creation; al-Jahiz, Kitab al-Hayawan; Lebling, Legends of the Fire Spirits; Encyclopaedia Iranica

name: Miraculous Well of Sidi Bou Said
description: The Miraculous Well of Sidi Bou Said is a legendary blessed water source in the famous blue-and-white Tunisian town of Sidi Bou Said, near Tunis. According to local legend, the well was blessed by Sidi Bou Said (also known as Abu Said al-Baji), a 13th-century Sufi saint who lived and taught in the area. The well is said to possess miraculous healing powers, with locals and visitors alike claiming that drinking water from it can cure various ailments, from simple headaches to more serious diseases. The saint, after whom the town is named, was a respected Islamic scholar and mystic known for his piety and miraculous works. The legend holds that he blessed the well so that his followers would always have access to healing water. The well has become a pilgrimage site for those seeking cures and blessings. The story reflects the widespread North African tradition of maraboutism—the veneration of holy figures (marabouts or wali) whose blessings are believed to continue after their death, often associated with specific locations like wells, springs, or trees
source: Carthage Magazine; Tunisian oral traditions

name: Sieidi Spirit
description: Sieidi (also seita) spirits are the spiritual forces dwelling in unusual rock formations, stones, or landscape features considered sacred in Sami religion. Each family or clan had its local sieidi — a naturally shaped stone or rock formation that was the dwelling place of a spirit with power over local animals, fish, and birds. Offerings of reindeer meat, antlers, horns, fish, and metal objects were made at these sites for hunting luck, protection, and general prosperity. Some sieidis were so holy that one had to approach them on hands and knees. In Inari, Finland, there were 17 known seita sites. The sieidi was not itself a god but a place where spiritual power resided; the spirit inhabiting it was a form of háldi. Sieidis were systematically destroyed by Christian missionaries, and shaman drums were burned. Despite this, offerings are still occasionally made at known sieidi sites, showing the persistence of Sami spiritual traditions
source: Wikipedia (Sami mythology); samimuseum.fi; MDPI Religions 2021

name: Siguanaba
description: La Siguanaba is one of the most famous figures in Salvadoran folklore — a shapeshifting spirit that appears as a beautiful long-haired woman from behind but reveals the face of a horse or skull when she turns around. According to Salvadoran legend, she was originally Sihuehuet (Beautiful Woman), a peasant girl who used her charms and witchcraft to marry Yeisun, son of Tláloc. After her husband went to war, she had affairs and gave birth to Cipitio. She tried to poison her husband to claim the throne for her lover, but the plan backfired, transforming him into a giant monster. The god Teotl cursed her to wander eternally as the Siguanaba — beautiful at first sight but hideous upon approach. She now appears to unfaithful men, luring them to isolated gorges before revealing her true terrifying face. She is most often seen near rivers, washing clothes or bathing, always searching for her son Cipitio
source: Salvadoran oral tradition; snip Wikipedia (Sihuanaba); snip Mythical Encyclopedia

name: Si'lat
description: The Si'lat (plural: Si'lat) is a female class of jinn in Levantine and Palestinian folklore, distinct from both the ghoul and ordinary jinn. Unlike the shapeshifting ghoul, the Si'lat has an invariable form — it is a witchlike spirit of fixed appearance and is extremely treacherous. In Palestinian tradition, the Si'lat is considered one of the most dangerous types of jinn because of its cunning and malicious intelligence. It is particularly associated with causing madness, leading travelers astray in wilderness areas, and interfering with human affairs out of pure spite. Unlike jinn that can be reasoned with or placated, the Si'lat is irredeemably evil and delights in causing suffering. The Si'lat class of jinn is mentioned in medieval Arabic demonological texts alongside the Ghoul, the Ifrit, and the Marid
source: Saudi Arabian folklore — spirit documented in Arabian oral tradition.

name: Simurgh
description: Simurgh is a colossal benevolent mythical bird in Azerbaijani folklore, shared with Persian and broader Turkic mythology. This wise and ancient creature possesses profound healing powers and esoteric knowledge. The Simurgh nests atop the mythical Qaf Mountain at the edge of the world and is said to have lived so long that it witnessed the destruction of the world three times. In Azerbaijani tales, the Simurgh appears at moments of greatest despair to rescue heroes trapped in deep pits or remote mountains, carrying them to safety and imparting wisdom. Its feathers have miraculous healing properties. The Simurgh represents the harmony between nature, wisdom, and divine goodness, standing in eternal opposition to dark forces like the Divs In Azerbaijan folklore, this figure is known among the Azerbaijan people.
source: Azerbaijani/Persian mythology; the Simurgh is a colossal benevolent bird.

name: Singbonga (Supreme God of the Munda)
description: Singbonga is the supreme creator god in the traditional religion of the Munda people, one of India's largest Adivasi (indigenous tribal) communities primarily living in the Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal regions. According to Munda creation mythology, before the universe existed, there was nothing but water. Singbonga, whose name means 'Sun God' or 'Great Spirit Sun,' floated above this primordial ocean and set a cosmic egg afloat on its surface. From this egg hatched the first beings — Horo the tortoise and Karakom the crab. The tortoise dove deep into the waters and brought earth to the surface on his back. But the earth was too soft, so Singbonga created a great spider that wove a web across the landscape, solidifying the earth into firm land. Singbonga then created the first humans, the sun, the moon, the stars, and all living things. The Munda creation story emphasizes cooperative effort between Singbonga and animals rather than top-down divine command, reflecting the tribe's communitarian values. Singbonga is considered the source of all life, the giver of rain and sunshine, and the ultimate moral authority. He is approached through intermediary spirits called bongas
source: Munda oral traditions, Sarna religion, tribal folklore of Jharkhand

name: Sirdalsjøormen
description: Sirdalsjøormen is a lake serpent or sea monster said to inhabit the connected lakes of Sirdalsvannet and Lundevannet in the Sirdal valley of Sørlandet. The serpent is described as having a horse-like head, a long neck, and a dark body that creates wakes as it moves through the water. It was believed to travel between the two lakes through underground channels. Multiple witness reports have been recorded from the 1800s to modern times, with the last reported observation in November 2016. Local folklorist Berner Eikeland interviewed many informants about their sightings in the 1950s. The Sirdalsjøormen is part of a broader Norwegian tradition of inland lake serpents (like Selbusjøormen in Trøndelag and the Storsjøoddyret) adapted to Sørlandet's specific geography. The serpent was considered generally harmless unless provoked
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Siv Yis (Shee Yee — First Hmong Shaman)
description: Siv Yis (also spelled Shee Yee or Siv Yig) is the legendary first shaman in Hmong mythology who received shamanic power from the spirit world and taught it to humanity. According to the Hmong creation myth, in ancient times the evil spirit Ntxwj Nyog (Ndu Nyong) brought sickness and death to humanity. The high god Yawm Saub (Yer Shau) sent Siv Yis down to earth to combat Ntxwj Nyog and retrieve stolen souls. Siv Yis learned the sacred rituals, chants, and healing practices from the spirits — how to beat the drum to call spirits, swing the rattle bells (nyiaj cuam) to open gates between worlds, and sacrifice animals to pay the spirit debt. He successfully healed the sick and retrieved lost souls. During a final battle with Ntxwj Nyog, the evil spirit tricked Siv Yis into eating his own son's soul. In grief, Siv Yis left the human world, but before departing, he scattered his shamanic tools across the earth, declaring they would work for those who followed his ways. Today, Hmong shamans call themselves Siv Yis when in trance, channeling his power
source: Hmong oral tradition — Siv Yis culture hero and shaman.

name: Skarsfjellgubben
description: Skarsfjellgubben (also known as Sømnakongen, the King of Sømna) is an old troll king from Nordland folklore who saved Lekamøya from Hestmannen's attack. When Hestmannen shot an arrow at Lekamøya as she fled, Skarsfjellgubben threw his broad-brimmed hat into the path of the arrow. The arrow pierced the hat, creating a massive hole through it. Skarsfjellgubben, his hat, the arrow, and Lekamøya all turned to stone at sunrise. The hat became Torghatten — the famous mountain with a distinctive hole through it on Torget island near Brønnøysund. The hole is 160 meters long, 35 meters high, and 20 meters wide. Torghatten is one of Norway's most famous natural landmarks. Skarsfjellgubben represents wisdom and protective elder power in the Seven Sisters legend cycle. His quick thinking saved Lekamøya
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Skeljaskrímsli
description: Skeljaskrímsli (Shell Monster) is a quadrupedal coastal monster from Icelandic folklore, about the size of a bull calf or large horse. Its entire body is covered in a thick coat of shells that rattle loudly as it walks. The creature emits a powerful stench, has reddish eyes, and a phosphorescent glow from its mouth. It has a long tail with a lump or hook at the end. Its blood is toxic. Skeljaskrímsli hauls onto shore on moonless winter nights, attracted to light. It leaves deep gouges in farmhouse doors and walls where it tries to enter. Despite its terrifying appearance, the skeljaskrímsli is not always aggressive — it seems more curious than predatory. However, its toxic blood and powerful stench make it dangerous to approach. The creature is found in Icelandic folklore collections and represents the deep-seated fear of strange coastal creatures washing ashore
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Skeljungur
description: Skeljungur (Shell-Whale) is a unique illhveli (evil whale) in Icelandic folklore distinguished by being covered in rattling shells and being the only edible wicked whale. Skeljungur is 20-45 meters long, fat-bodied, with short flippers and no dorsal fin. Its body is covered with shells that rattle loudly as it moves — the sound gives it away. It sleeps vertically with its head above water. The shells make it constantly itchy, so it rubs its head against coastal rocks. Skeljungur actively blocks ships and flips them with its fins. Despite being classified as an illhveli (evil whale), its flesh was considered edible, though very dangerous to obtain. Skeljungur has a particular hatred for the sound of iron being filed — it will beach itself to escape the noise, making it the only illhveli that can be driven ashore. Described in Konungs skuggsjá and later Icelandic folk tradition
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Skifting
description: Skiftingen (also called Bytting) is the Danish changeling — a troll or Bjergfolk infant secretly exchanged for a human baby. The changeling is ugly, sickly, never grows, and has an enormous appetite. It cries constantly but also shows unnaturally adult intelligence — it may speak in rhymes, comment on ancient events, or demonstrate knowledge no infant should possess. The most famous Danish changeling story involves a child who, when the mother brewed beer in an eggshell to test it, exclaimed: 'I have seen Rold Forest cut down twice and grow up thrice, but never saw such a long brewing!' giving itself away. The changeling could be forced to leave by: brewing in an eggshell, threatening to slaughter a pig at an unusual hour, or beating the child with a birch rod on Ash Wednesday. The Bjergfolk mother would then return the human child
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Skoffín
description: Skoffín is a deadly hybrid creature in Icelandic folklore, born from the mating of a male Arctic fox and a female tabby cat. The skoffín is partially hairless with bald patches and possesses a deadly gaze — everything it looks at dies instantly. Animals, humans, and even plants wither under its stare. The skoffín changes color with the seasons like the Arctic fox: white in winter, brown in summer. It can only be killed with silver bullets or by showing it its own reflection in a mirror — causing it to die from its own gaze. The creature was considered extremely rare but devastating when encountered. One famous story tells of a skoffín that killed all livestock on a farm before the farmer trapped it and showed it its reflection in a polished silver plate. The skoffín tradition is unique to Iceland and shows how the Arctic environment shaped folklore about hybrid animals
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Skotta
description: Skotta (meaning Tail) is a specific type of female ghost in Icelandic folklore named for the distinctive tail-like appearance of her headdress hanging down her back. Skotta wears the traditional Icelandic Faldbúningur headdress but backward — the long tail of the headdress hangs down her back like a tail (skott). She wears rust-red headwear, red socks, and is often described sucking her fingers or chewing on her own hair. Skotta attaches herself to specific people, families, or even entire towns, following them and causing misfortune. She is a type of afturganga (one who walks again after death) — a person who was wronged or died under unusual circumstances and returned to haunt the living. Skotta was particularly associated with the Snæfellsnes peninsula and the Westfjords. Unlike the Norwegian ghost traditions, Skotta has specific clothing identifying her as an Icelandic ghost — her backward headdress is the key feature
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Skuggabaldur
description: Skuggabaldur (Shadow Baldur) is a hybrid creature in Icelandic folklore, the opposite cross of the skoffín — born from a tomcat and a vixen (female fox). Skuggabaldur has very dark fur, almost black, and sometimes possesses the same deadly gaze as the skoffín. It preys primarily on livestock. The most famous skuggabaldur story involves one that was killed by a farmer. When it was dying, the creature spoke and said: Tell the tomcat at Bollastaðir. The farmer later passed on the message at Bollastaðir farm. When he spoke the words, a tomcat attacked and killed him by biting his throat. This legend illustrates the Icelandic belief that hybrid creatures had supernatural connections and that messages from dying monsters should not be delivered. Skuggabaldur, like skoffín, is part of the uniquely Icelandic tradition of fox-cat hybrids that combines domestic and wild animal traits into supernatural creatures
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Snåsavettern
description: Snåsavettern (the Snåsa Water Wight) is a water spirit said to inhabit Snåsavatnet, the largest lake in Trøndelag with an area of 125 square kilometers, located in Snåsa municipality. Like many large Norwegian lakes, Snåsavatnet was believed to have its own vette (nature spirit) that protected the lake and all the life within it. The Snåsavettern is a type of water vette that controls the fish population, the weather on the lake, and the safety of those who travel across it. It could grant excellent fishing to respectful fishermen or create dangerous waves and sudden storms to punish those who overfished or disrespected the lake. Offerings of the first catch of the season were traditionally thrown back into the lake to honor the Snåsavettern. Sami influence from the nearby Snåsa reindeer herding areas may have shaped the legend as well, blending Norse and Sami nature spirit traditions
source: Scandinavian folklore; Vættir are nature spirits of the land and water.

name: Sogolon
description: Sogolon is the mother of Sundiata Keita and a central figure in the Epic of Sundiata. Known as the "Buffalo Woman," she was originally a mysterious and dangerous being — a buffalo that terrorized the land of Do. Two hunter brothers discovered she was a woman transformed by a curse. They captured her, and one brother married her. Sogolon was described as ugly and hunchbacked, and King Maghan Kon Fatta married her on the advice of a soothsayer who prophesied that her son would become a great king. Despite persecution by the king's first wife, Sogolon protected and raised Sundiata. Her strength, patience, and determination shaped Sundiata's character. After fleeing into exile, she pushed Sundiata to fulfill his destiny. The Mandinka saying "the child is worth no more than the mother is worth" reflects Sogolon's importance
source: Mande epic; Sogolon is the mother of Sundiata, known as the buffalo-woman.

name: Dhegdheer
description: Dhegdheer, meaning 'Long Ear' in Somali, is a fearsome cannibalistic demon from Somali folklore who hunts in forests and preys primarily on lost or wandering children. Once a mortal woman whose selfishness and greed led a curse to transform her into a monster, Dhegdheer possesses supernatural hearing that allows her to detect even the faintest sounds from great distances. She is closely associated with the Hargega Valley and the Caves of Xargega in the Sanaag region of northern Somalia. Her legend is so deeply embedded in Somali culture that children are warned not to wander far from home lest Dhegdheer snatch them. Her daughter Buuti features in stories as a heroic figure who defies her cannibalistic mother's nature to save innocent villagers. Dhegdheer eventually meets her end when the forces of natural justice drown her in a river, returning peace to the land
source: Somali Oral Tradition

name: Qori-Ismaris
description: Qori-Ismaris (literally 'the stick-rubber') is a legendary figure from Somali mythology known as the Hyena-Man, the Somali equivalent of the Western werewolf. According to traditional belief, Qori-Ismaris was a man who possessed the dark power to transform into a hyena by rubbing a magical stick on his hindquarters at nightfall. Before dawn, he would repeat the same action to reverse the transformation and return to human shape. Some versions of the legend elevate Qori-Ismaris to an immortal witch-queen who wanders the desert disguised as a beautiful woman, luring travelers into illusions and guiding them to their doom. The figure represents the dangerous boundary between human and animal, civilization and wilderness. Stories of Qori-Ismaris served as warnings about strangers who might not be what they appear, especially those met at twilight—the liminal hour when transformations occurred. The legend reflects deep cultural anxieties about deception, the untamed wilderness, and the animal nature lurking beneath human civility
source: Wikipedia - Somali mythology; YouTube - Qori Ismaris; Somalispot forum; The Daily Somalia

name: Sơn Tinh (Mountain Spirit)
description: Sơn Tinh (literally 'Mountain Spirit' or 'Mountain God') is the powerful deity of the mountains in Vietnamese mythology, specifically associated with Mount Tản Viên (Ba Vì) in northern Vietnam. According to legend, during the reign of the 18th Hùng King, the king's beautiful daughter Mỵ Nương was sought in marriage by two suitors: Sơn Tinh (the mountain spirit) and Thủy Tinh (the water spirit). The king set a challenge — whoever arrived first with the prescribed wedding gifts would win his daughter. Sơn Tinh arrived first with gifts including ivory, gold, and rare mountain treasures, and married the princess. The enraged Thủy Tinh raised floods to destroy the mountains, but Sơn Tinh used his power to raise the peaks higher. Their eternal struggle represents the annual monsoon floods that strike Vietnam's Red River Delta. The myth explains both the region's seasonal flooding and the Vietnamese people's resilience against nature
source: Vietnamese folk religion — Sơn Tinh mountain god.

name: Sotho Ancestral Ghosts (Matsatsi)
description: Sotho ghosts, often called matsatsi, are believed to be the spirits of ancestors who have not found peace in the afterlife. In Basotho mythology of Lesotho, death is not the end of existence but a transition to another realm, where the ancestors (badimo) continue to influence the living world. Most ancestors are benevolent protectors, but those who died violently, were not properly buried, or who harbor unresolved grievances may become restless ghosts that wander the earth. These spirits are often marked by unusual occurrences, strange sounds, cold spots, or apparitions. The mountainous terrain of Lesotho, with its misty valleys and remote passes, is considered particularly active with ghostly activity. The Basotho people maintain elaborate rituals to honor their ancestors and ensure their peaceful rest, including animal sacrifice, beer offerings, and consultation with traditional diviners. The belief in ghosts reinforces the importance of proper burial rituals and the maintenance of family bonds beyond death
source: Lesotho NewsDesk; Basotho oral traditions

name: Soucouyant
description: The Soucouyant is well-known in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines folklore as a shape-shifting, blood-sucking hag. As documented by Charles Day in his 19th-century book 'Five Years in the West Indies' and referenced in the Know Your Caribbean Podcast, Vincentian tradition holds that the Soucouyant sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire. In Saint Vincent, belief in the Soucouyant is intertwined with the practice of Obeah, which remains a powerful force in Vincentian spiritual life. The creature is said to be a reclusive old woman by day who transforms at night to drain the blood of her victims. Vincentians traditionally protect their homes by placing salt in doorways and hanging garlic over entrances. The legend reinforces the importance of community surveillance and the dangers of dabbling in black magic
source: Caribbean folklore — the Soucouyant vampire documented across Caribbean oral tradition.

name: Garang
description: Garang is the first man in Dinka mythology of South Sudan, created alongside Abuk, the first woman, by the supreme creator Nhialic. According to Dinka creation tradition, Nhialic formed Garang and Abuk from the rich clay of Sudan, then placed them in a huge pot. When the creator opened the pot, Garang and Abuk emerged as fully formed human beings. Nhialic gave them only one grain of corn each per day for sustenance, which left them perpetually hungry. When Abuk began hoarding and planting grain for agriculture, the creator was displeased, but this act of innovation ultimately shaped human civilization. Garang represents the first human male in Dinka cosmology and, together with Abuk, establishes the foundation of Dinka lineage and society. Unlike Abuk who has specific symbols and continued worship, Garang is primarily significant as the male half of the primordial pair. Their children included Deng, the powerful god of rain and fertility, making Garang the ancestor of a divine lineage as well as humanity
source: Britannica - Garang; Wikipedia - Abuk (mythology); Encyclopedia.com; paanluelwel.com

name: Springand-Annbjør
description: Springand-Annbjør (Running Annbjør) is a restless running spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. She is described as a female undead or wraith that runs endlessly through the Setesdal valley, never stopping, never resting. The name Annbjør is a female name common in Setesdal, and the legend likely originated as a ghost story about a specific woman condemned to eternal running as punishment for a grave sin. Springand-Annbjør runs along the roads and paths between the farms of the valley, always at night, always alone. Those who see her say she runs with desperate speed, her feet barely touching the ground, her breath coming in ragged gasps. She cannot speak or stop. If someone tries to speak to her, she simply runs past. Seeing Springand-Annbjør was considered an omen — of death, disaster, or simply a reminder of one's own mortality. The spirit is documented in Johannes Skar's supranormal catalog in Gamalt or Setesdal
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Stökkull
description: Stökkull (the Jumper) is the most feared of all the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic folklore, despite not being the largest. Stökkull has a distinctive rounded body, dark above and white below, 8-20 meters long, with a battering-ram snout. Its most remarkable feature is the flaps of skin (blinders) that cover its eyes — it must leap completely out of the water to see. According to Navigatio Sancti Brendani, Saint Brendan prayed to God to give Stökkull these blinders to limit its destructive power. When Stökkull leaps, it pile-drives ships underneath it, smashing them to pieces. The sight of Stökkull breaching was the most terrifying thing an Icelandic sailor could witness. The jumper whale is unique to Icelandic tradition and represents the danger of breaching whales combined with supernatural malevolence. The blinders motif shows how Christian hagiography adapted native folklore
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Stállo
description: Stállo is a giant from Sami mythology. He is evil, strong, and dangerous but also clumsy, stupid, and easily tricked by clever Sami heroes who invariably outwit him using intelligence over brute force. He dresses in dark clothes with gold buttons and carries a rucksack on his back and a sharp knife. Stállo can be created by noaidis (shamans) from earth, wood, or turf, given part of the shaman's own life force, and sent to attack enemies. If killed with his own knife, he gains strength instead of dying. He whistles sharply when approaching, and hearing his pipe or whistle in the wind is a dangerous omen. He lives in mountains near Sami settlements, demanding reindeer sacrifices. The Stállo tradition may originate from historical encounters with Norse Vikings, Karelian raiders, or Russian tax collectors, who wore steel (stål) armor
source: Wikipedia (Stallo); SNL.no; Helgeland Museum; eldar-heide.net; levandekulturarv.se

name: Stiklestadsgjenferden
description: Stiklestadsgjenferden (the Stiklestad Ghosts) are the spectral apparitions said to haunt the Stiklestad battlefield in Verdal, Trøndelag. The Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 was one of the most significant battles in Norwegian history, where King Olav Haraldsson (later Saint Olav) fell. According to local tradition, the ghosts of the fallen soldiers reappear on the anniversary of the battle, reenacting the fight in the mist that rises from the low-lying fields. The phenomenon is most often reported on July 29 (Olsok, the feast of St. Olav) when mist conditions are right. Locals have reported seeing shadowy figures, hearing clashing weapons and battle cries, and feeling an eerie presence in the area. The legend is documented in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling as entry ml4015 (De dødes messe) from Verdal, collected by Anton Røstad
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Stállo
description: Stállo is the most iconic antagonist in Sami folklore — a large, human-like cannibal giant who eats people, especially children. He is evil, strong, and dangerous but also clumsy, stupid, and easily tricked by clever Sami heroes who invariably outwit him using intelligence over brute force. He dresses in dark clothes with gold buttons and carries a rucksack on his back and a sharp knife. Stállo can be created by noaidis (shamans) from earth, wood, or turf, given part of the shaman's own life force, and sent to attack enemies. If killed with his own knife, he gains strength instead of dying. He whistles sharply when approaching, and hearing his pipe or whistle in the wind is a dangerous omen. He lives in mountains near Sami settlements, demanding reindeer sacrifices. The Stállo tradition may originate from historical encounters with Norse Vikings, Karelian raiders, or Russian tax collectors, who wore steel (stål) armor
source: Sami folklore; the Stallo is a malevolent, often cannibalistic giant in Sami tradition.

name: Stállo
description: Stállo is a giant from Sápmi mythology. He is evil, strong, and dangerous but also clumsy, stupid, and easily tricked by clever Sami heroes who invariably outwit him using intelligence over brute force. He dresses in dark clothes with gold buttons and carries a rucksack on his back and a sharp knife. Stállo can be created by noaidis (shamans) from earth, wood, or turf, given part of the shaman's own life force, and sent to attack enemies. If killed with his own knife, he gains strength instead of dying. He whistles sharply when approaching, and hearing his pipe or whistle in the wind is a dangerous omen. He lives in mountains near Sami settlements, demanding reindeer sacrifices. The Stállo tradition may originate from historical encounters with Norse Vikings, Karelian raiders, or Russian tax collectors, who wore steel (stål) armor
source: Sami folklore; the Stallo is a malevolent, often cannibalistic giant in Sami tradition.

name: Storjunkare
description: Storjunkare are sacred stone beings in Sami religion — unusually shaped stones or rock formations resembling humans or animals that were set up on mountaintops, in caves, or near rivers and lakes as objects of worship. The term comes from Scandinavian Sami tradition and describes large, sacred stones that were treated as living spirits. Honor was done to them by spreading fresh twigs under them in winter and leaves or grass in summer. They had power over all animals, fish, and birds, and granted good luck to those who hunted or fished for them. Reindeer were sacrificed at these sites, and every clan and family had its own hill of sacrifice dedicated to its local Storjunkare. According to the mid-18th century work Cérémonies et coutumes religieuses de tous les peuples du monde, Storjunkare was the second member of a Sami trinity after Tiermes (the thunder god), with Baivre or Jumala as the third member. Unlike sieidis which were natural formations, Storjunkare were sometimes deliberately set up stones that were then worshipped
source: Wikipedia (Sami mythology); Cérémonies et coutumes religieuses (1750s); MDPI Religions 2021

name: Åland Storm-Witch
description: The storm-witch of Åland is a female practitioner of weather magic who possesses the secret art of tying the wind into knots of rope. Unlike malevolent hags who conjure storms through incantations, the Åland storm-witch operates as a trader of winds: she sells sailors knotted ropes that release favorable breezes when untied. Untying one knot produces a light wind, untying two fills the sails, but untying all three awakens a devastating tempest. This tradition is inextricably linked to Kastelholm Castle, the 14th-century fortress at the heart of the main island, where during the 1665–1668 Kastelholm witch trials storm-witches were among the accused. The practice reflects the deep dependence of Åland’s islanders on safe sea passage — the archipelago’s thousands of islands, skerries, and open Baltic stretches made weather control a matter of life and death. The tradition persists in local memory: even today, some islanders refuse to throw knotted rope into the sea without cutting the knots first, for fear of stirring the winds that should sleep
source: Åland folklore, Kastelholm witch trial records, Baltic maritime tradition

name: Suliskongen
description: Suliskongen (the King of Sulitjelma) is the troll king of the Sulitjelma mountains in Nordland, and the father of the legendary Seven Sisters — Botnkrona, Grytfoten, Skjeringen, Tvillingene (the Twins), Kvasstinden, and Breitinden. According to legend, Suliskongen sent his seven daughters away from their home in Sulitjelma to the island of Landegode for discipline. When Hestmannen pursued them across the sea, the sisters danced on Alsten island to distract him. They were caught by the sunrise and turned into the seven peaks that form the distinctive silhouette of the Seven Sisters mountain range near Sandnessjøen. Suliskongen himself watches from his throne in the Sulitjelma mountains near the Swedish border. The Seven Sisters mountain range is one of Norway's most famous landmarks, and the legend is the best-known troll story in Northern Norway
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Sumanguru Kante
description: Sumanguru Kanté is the villainous sorcerer-king of the Sosso people in the Epic of Sundiata. He was a powerful king who seized the remnants of the Ghana Empire and conquered nine neighboring kingdoms, including the Mandinka lands. Sumanguru was a master blacksmith and powerful sorcerer, invulnerable to all weapons except one — an arrow tipped with a white rooster spur. He possessed a magical balafon (xylophone) that could reveal his enemies' secrets. His seven-story tower palace in Sosso was filled with fetishes and magical charms. Sumanguru forced the Mandinka into brutal submission until Sundiata Keita returned from exile. At the Battle of Kirina, Sundiata's magic arrow struck Sumanguru, who fled into the Koulikoro mountains and vanished. The epic portrays Sumanguru as a tyrant whose cruelty necessitated the rise of the Mali Empire
source: Mande oral tradition, Epic of Sundiata, Wikipedia

name: Sundiata Keita
description: Sundiata Keita was the legendary founder of the Mali Empire, the greatest empire in West African history. Born crippled and unable to walk, Sundiata was the son of King Maghan Kon Fatta and the ugly, hunchbacked woman Sogolon. A prophecy foretold his greatness. After his father's death, Sundiata and his mother were persecuted and forced into exile. In exile, he miraculously learned to walk and grew into a powerful warrior. Meanwhile, the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kanté conquered the Mandinka people. Recalled from exile, Sundiata forged a coalition of kingdoms and defeated Soumaoro at the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235) using a magic arrow tipped with a white cock's spur — Soumaoro's only vulnerability. Sundiata became the first Mansa of the Mali Empire, establishing the Kouroukan Fouga constitution and building an empire that thrived for centuries
source: Mande epic; Sundiata Keita is the founder of the Mali Empire.

name: Suniyam Demon (Sinhalese Sorcery Spirit)
description: Suniyam is the chief demon of sorcery and black magic in Sinhalese folklore, believed to be one of the most powerful and dangerous of the Yaksha spirits. According to legend, Suniyam was once a Yaksha who served the god Vishnu but was cursed for his arrogance or misdeeds, becoming the master of all dark arts and sorcery. He governs all forms of black magic (kodivina), curses (sapa), and bewitchments (vas kavi). In the hierarchy of Sinhalese demons, Suniyam is considered the chief (pradhana) of all disease-bringing and misfortune-causing demons, commanding the other yakshas of the Daha Ata Sanniya (the eighteen maladies). He is associated with madness, epilepsy, chronic illness, business failure, family disputes, and all forms of inexplicable misfortune. When a Sinhalese person suffers a series of unexplained calamities, it is often attributed to Suniyam's influence, believed to have been sent by an enemy through a sorcerer (kattadiya or yaddura). Counteracting Suniyam's power requires the most elaborate and expensive exorcism ceremonies, often involving multiple nights of rituals, food offerings, and the construction of elaborate altars
source: Sinhalese Tovil exorcism traditions, Bruce Kapferer 'A Celebration of Demons', Sinhala folk religion

name: Shurpanakha (Rakshasi)
description: Shurpanakha ('she whose fingernails are like winnowing fans') is a rakshasi (demoness) in the Hindu epic Ramayana, sister of the Lankan king Ravana and daughter of sage Vishrava and the rakshasi Kaikeshi. Her role in the epic, though small, is pivotal — her encounter with Rama and Lakshmana in the Panchavati forest triggered the chain of events leading to Sita's abduction and the great war of Lanka. According to Valmiki's Ramayana, she was widowed when Ravana killed her husband, the Danava prince Vidyutjihva. While wandering the forests, she encountered the exiled prince Rama and became infatuated with him. When Rama and Lakshmana rejected her advances, she attacked Sita, and Lakshmana cut off her nose. Humiliated, she fled to her brother Khara and later to Ravana, whose desire to avenge her led to Sita's kidnapping. Despite her demonic nature, some versions of the epic, particularly the Kamba Ramayanam, portray her as a tragic figure driven by loneliness and love
source: Valmiki Ramayana (Aranya Kanda), Kamba Ramayanam, various Ramayana adaptations

name: Svartalv (Swedish)
description: Svartálfar (black elves or dark elves) are supernatural beings from Norse cosmology who dwell underground in Svartálfheim, the world of the black elves. They are described as the light-avoiding counterparts to the Ljósálfar (light elves) who live in Álfheim. In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, the svartálfar appear to be synonymous with the dwarves (dvergar), and Svartálfheim is considered interchangeable with Niðavellir (Dark Fields). The svartálfar are renowned as master craftspeople, and among their most famous creations are the Sons of Ivaldi's work: Sif's golden hair, Freyr's ship Skíðblaðnir, and Odin's spear Gungnir. They are described as pitch-black in appearance, turning to stone if exposed to daylight, and dwelling in underground forges and mines. In later Swedish folklore tradition, svartálfar merged with concepts of underjordiska and were sometimes blamed for nightmares — the German word for nightmare, Albtraum, literally means "elf-dream."
source: Prose Edda by Snorri Sturluson

name: Taleju Bhawani (Royal Goddess of the Malla Kings)
description: Taleju Bhawani is a fearsome tantric form of the goddess Durga who served as the royal tutelary deity of the Malla kings of the Kathmandu Valley. According to legend, she was the patron goddess who granted sovereignty to the Malla dynasty. The most famous story recounts that King Jayaprakash Malla of Kathmandu played dice nightly with the goddess, who appeared in the form of a beautiful woman. The king was forbidden to reveal this secret to anyone. One night, the king's daughter discovered them, and the enraged goddess vanished, declaring she would never return to the palace in that form. However, she appeared to the king in a dream, instructing him to worship a virgin girl of the Shakya clan as her living embodiment — thus establishing the Kumari tradition. Taleju is associated with the Shri Yantra, the most sacred of all tantric diagrams, and her worship involves secret tantric rituals conducted by Rajopadhyaya and Karmacharya priests. Her grand temple in Kathmandu Durbar Square is one of the most architecturally impressive structures in the valley, built by King Mahendra Malla in 1564. Taleju represents both spiritual authority and the political sovereignty of Nepalese kingship
source: Taleju Bhawani temple history, Malla dynasty chronicles, Nepali Newar traditions

name: Tannit (Neith-Atheme)
description: Tannit (also known as Neith, Tanit) is the supreme female deity of ancient Berber mythology, originating in Libya. She is considered the Libyan Triple Goddess par excellence and is one of the oldest known goddess figures in North Africa. According to Berber mythology scholars, the Egyptian goddess Neith, the Phoenician goddess Tanit, and the Greek goddess Athena are all derived from the original Berber Tannit. She is a goddess of war, wisdom, fertility, and the cycles of life and death. Tannit was particularly venerated in the region of Libya and later became the patron goddess of Carthage. She is often depicted with a crescent moon on her forehead, associated with lunar cycles and the feminine principle. Her symbol—a circle above a triangle with a horizontal line—is one of the most recognizable religious symbols of the ancient world, found throughout Carthaginian sites in Tunisia and Libya. Tannit represents the indigenous Libyan foundation for many Mediterranean goddess traditions, highlighting the significant influence of Berber religion on neighboring cultures. Her worship included both protective and warlike aspects, and she was believed to provide guidance and protection in times of conflict
source: Temehu.com; Libyan Heritage House
